Style

Modernist architecture

947 buildings

Modernist architecture builds with new construction technology and rejects ornament, so volume, structure and plan carry the whole design. It emerged at the end of the 19th century and was dominant from the Second World War until the 1980s. In 1932 Hitchcock and Johnson's exhibition at MoMA set out its principles: architecture as volume, regularity in the facade rather than symmetry, and no applied ornament. Under the name International Style it spread throughout the world. Le Corbusier's white houses of the 1920s had no ornament inside or out.

Read moreShow less

The Fagus Factory in Alfeld (1911), by Walter Gropius and Adolf Meyer, sets its glass curtain wall forward of the piers, so the corners turn with no column. Gropius's Bauhaus Dessau (1926) wraps its workshops in glass on a pinwheel plan. Mies van der Rohe's Villa Tugendhat in Brno (1930) brings the open plan into a family home, with glass walls that drop away to the garden. Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye in Poissy (1931) puts his Five Points of Architecture into a single house. Mies's Seagram Building in New York (1958) stands back behind a plaza, its bronze mullions expressing the frame.

Questions students ask

What is modernist architecture?

Modernist architecture turns away from ornament and depends on new building technology, leaving volume, structure and plan to do all the design work. It appeared at the close of the 19th century, then was the leading approach from the Second World War to the 1980s, travelling worldwide as the International Style. In the 1920s, Le Corbusier's white houses carried no decoration on either their interiors or their exteriors.

What are the principles of modernist architecture?

Hitchcock and Johnson's 1932 exhibition at MoMA in New York set out three: buildings conceived as volume, a regular facade in place of symmetry, and no applied ornament. Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye (1931) shows them in practice, combining his Five Points of Architecture in one house, as does the Barcelona Pavilion (1929), where freestanding walls beneath a floating roof let space flow.

Which modernist buildings should architecture students study?

In date order, a short list: the Fagus Factory in Alfeld (1911), where the glass wall wraps the corners without a column; Bauhaus Dessau (1926) and its pinwheel plan; the Barcelona Pavilion (1929); Villa Savoye (1931); Fallingwater (1939), cantilevered above a waterfall; and New York's Seagram Building (1958), set back from a plaza, with bronze mullions that show its frame.

Which modernist houses should I study?

Houses show modernism's ideas most clearly. Compare the Rietveld Schröder House in Utrecht (1924), De Stijl in three dimensions; Villa Tugendhat in Brno (1930), whose glass walls drop away to the garden; Fallingwater (1939); the Eames House in Los Angeles (1949), built from off-the-shelf industrial parts; Philip Johnson's Glass House (1949); and the Farnsworth House (1951), a single glass room lifted above a floodplain.
